articles.description: The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday. Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos has directed concerned agencies to ensure a peaceful, orderly and credible conduct of the BARMM polls on Sept. 14. Castro clarified that the reported killings in BARMM since the start of the year were not related to the upcoming polls, and instead involved personal conflicts, citing information from the Commission on Elections. She said the Comelec, Philippine National Police (PNP) and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) are conducting focused law enforcement operations against private armed groups and other security threats in the region. Marcos earlier assured the Bangsamoro people that the first parliamentary election would push through as scheduled. Castro said 8,299 PNP personnel would be deployed in BARMM for election security. She added that the number may be augmented as the election approaches, depending on the PNP’s threat assessment and the Comelec requirements. “The PNP is working alongside the AFP and the Philippine Coast Guard to boost security, particularly in election areas of concern identified by the Comelec, to ensure the safe, peaceful and orderly conduct of the election,” Castro said. Meanwhile, 12 people have been arrested for violating the Comelec gun ban, as security operations intensify. PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez said the arrests came as police continue implementing security measures during the campaign period, noting that no violent election-related incident has been reported so far. “We have already laid out and are implementing our security operations,” Nartatez said. text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday. Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos has directed concerned agencies to ensure a peaceful, orderly and credible conduct of the BARMM polls on Sept. 14. Marcos earlier assured the Bangsamoro people that the first parliamentary election would push through as scheduled. Castro said 8,299 PNP personnel would be deployed in BARMM for election security. She added that the number may be augmented as the election approaches, depending on the PNP’s threat assessment and the Comelec requirements. “The PNP is working alongside the AFP and the Philippine Coast Guard to boost security, particularly in election areas of concern identified by the Comelec, to ensure the safe, peaceful and orderly conduct of the election,” Castro said. Meanwhile, 12 people have been arrested for violating the Comelec gun ban, as security operations intensify. PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez said the arrests came as police continue implementing security measures during the campaign period, noting that no violent election-related incident has been reported so far. “We have already laid out and are implementing our security operations,” Nartatez said. text.preview: Lawyer Roderick Wamil, a former state auditor with the Commission on Audit’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO), returned to the witness stand on Tuesday to testify on the disbursement of more than P200 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) during Vice President Sara Duterte’s tenure as education secretary. Prosecution During the prosecution's presentation of evidence, Wamil testified that at least P129 million of the OVP's P250-million confidential fund allocation for the first and second quarters of 2023 lacked supporting documents proving that the disbursements were made for their intended purposes, in violation of Joint Circular No. 2015-01 governing the use of confidential and intelligence funds. According to Wamil, the unsupported disbursements included purchases of medicines and food assistance, as well as the payment of rewards and incentives for travel related to confidential operations, whose authenticity could not be verified due to the absence of the required documentation. articles.title: Palace: Reinforce security ahead of BARMM election
articles.description: The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday. Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos has directed concerned agencies to ensure a peaceful, orderly and credible conduct of the BARMM polls on Sept. 14. Castro clarified that the reported killings in BARMM since the start of the year were not related to the upcoming polls, and instead involved personal conflicts, citing information from the Commission on Elections. She said the Comelec, Philippine National Police (PNP) and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) are conducting focused law enforcement operations against private armed groups and other security threats in the region. Marcos earlier assured the Bangsamoro people that the first parliamentary election would push through as scheduled. Castro said 8,299 PNP personnel would be deployed in BARMM for election security. She added that the number may be augmented as the election approaches, depending on the PNP’s threat assessment and the Comelec requirements. “The PNP is working alongside the AFP and the Philippine Coast Guard to boost security, particularly in election areas of concern identified by the Comelec, to ensure the safe, peaceful and orderly conduct of the election,” Castro said. Meanwhile, 12 people have been arrested for violating the Comelec gun ban, as security operations intensify. PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez said the arrests came as police continue implementing security measures during the campaign period, noting that no violent election-related incident has been reported so far. “We have already laid out and are implementing our security operations,” Nartatez said. The RPO 14 of the Department of Justice covers the five provinces in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Maguindanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, and the cities of Lamitan, Marawi and Cotabato, where the BARMM regional capitol is located. Copies of the RPO 14's resolution pertaining to its case buildup against Nano, one of the 11 municipal mayors in Basilan, and several others, were obtained on Wednesday by reporters from officials of the Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Camp SK Pendatun in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte and the military’s Western Mindanao Command based in Zamboanga City. articles.title: Sara Duterte's impeachment trial, Week 5: Beyond the receipts
articles.description: Five weeks into the trial, the proceedings have become about more than the fate of one elected official. They have evolved into an examination of how the Philippine government accounts for billions of pesos in confidential funds and whether the existing safeguards are sufficient to protect public money from misuse.

text.preview: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. Three days of testimony from Commission on Audit auditor Roderick Wamil, formerly assigned to the agency’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office, has shifted the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte from a largely political spectacle into a searching examination of confidential fund safeguards. In the process, the Senate impeachment court has exposed not only the strengths and weaknesses of the prosecution’s case but also the institutional gaps that have long surrounded the auditing of secret government expenditures. The proceedings from Days 11 to 13 demonstrate why impeachment trials should never be judged by dramatic courtroom exchanges alone. Beneath the debate over acknowledgment receipts, unusual names and missing documents lies a more consequential question: Has the prosecution shown that Duterte committed an impeachable offense, or has it primarily revealed deficiencies in the government’s auditing framework? Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro repeatedly says the prosecution’s case does not hinge on whether the names were aliases or genuine persons. “The important issue is accountability. Public officials entrusted with confidential funds must account for how public money was spent,” she said in an online press briefing on Thursday. Wamil’s testimony unquestionably advanced the prosecution’s case. Drawing from his audit of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, he detailed what COA considered repeated violations of Joint Circular No. 2015-01 — crafted in 2015 by COA, Department of Budget and Management, Department of the Interior and Local Government, the Government Commission for Government-Owned and Controlled Corporations, and the Department of National Defense — governing confidential and intelligence funds. articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial, Week 8: Who knew where the confidential funds went?
articles.description: Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent.

text.preview: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. The eighth week of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial ended with the Senate impeachment court focusing on a basic question: Who knew where the P500 million confidential funds went? Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent. Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio, the OVP assistant chief of staff, gave the most important testimony of the week. He told the court that Duterte knew about and authorized the activities involving confidential funds under her office. Asked by Presiding Officer Francis Escudero whether Duterte knew, supervised and authorized the entire process, from requesting the funds and withdrawing them to their release, spending, liquidation and responses to the Commission on Audit, Ortonio answered: “Yes, Your Honor.” His testimony followed two days of questioning of Gina Acosta, Duterte’s former special disbursing officer, now a staff officer VI at the OVP. A system of trust, or a break in accountability? Acosta said she released P125 million in cash to Lachica on Duterte’s instructions in December 2022. The money was the first tranche of the P500 million in OVP confidential funds now under scrutiny, disbursed from December 2022 to September 2023. But Acosta admitted that she did not personally know how Lachica spent the money. She said she relied on the documents he gave her when she prepared the liquidation reports. The prosecution has questioned whether this arrangement broke the chain of accountability for public funds. articles.title: Who are the COA witnesses testifying on Sara Duterte confidential funds? | ABS-CBN News
articles.description: On the sixth week of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the prosecution presented two witnesses from the Commission on Audit: Roderick Wamil

text.preview: State auditors Xylene Mae del Campo and Roderick Wamil. Maria Tan, ABS-CBN News MANILA — On the sixth week of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the prosecution presented two witnesses from the Commission on Audit: Roderick Wamil and Xylene Mae del Campo. Who is Roderick Wamil? Wamil, 34, currently serves as an audit team leader at COA-Pasay City. He has been with the commission for more than 11 years, having joined in 2014. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Accountancy from Central Luzon State University and his Juris Doctor degree from Arellano University. Before assuming his current post, Wamil served as a state auditor under the COA-Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO). WRAP: Tense exchanges as state auditor Wamil wraps up testimony His testimony focused on his experience auditing confidential fund disbursements, a key part of the prosecution's effort to establish alleged irregularities under Article I, which accuses Duterte of misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds. Wamil audited the Office of the Vice President's (OVP) liquidation of confidential funds for the fourth quarter of 2022 and the first, second, and third quarters of 2023. He also audited the Department of Education’s confidential funds during the first three quarters of 2023, when Duterte concurrently served as Education secretary. In February 2024, Wamil was reassigned to another office within the COA. Who is Xylene Mae del Campo? Following Wamil’s testimony, the prosecution presented its second COA witness, Xylene Mae del Campo. Del Campo, 36, is as a state auditor at the COA-ICFAO, succeeding Wamil in the position. She took over the audits of the OVP and DepEd confidential funds after Wamil’s transfer in February 2024. articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is 'evidence of success' in the use of confidential funds?
articles.description: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has entered its second month, with the Senate impeachment court now delving into the technical details surrounding the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Article I.

text.preview: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has entered its second month, with the Senate impeachment court now delving into the technical details surrounding the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Article I. One of the key terms that surfaced during the proceedings is "evidence of success." What does "evidence of success" mean? The term came up during the prosecution's questioning of state auditor Roderick Wamil, formerly of the Commission on Audit Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO), the office that audited confidential and intelligence funds lodged with various government offices, including the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) under Duterte. During direct examination, Wamil testified that the OVP reported spending P42 million in confidential funds for the provision of medical and food aid from February 6 to March 29, 2023, and another P40 million for the same purpose from April 25 to June 30, 2023, for a total of P82 million. "Our findings, or observations, were that the OVP did not submit documentary evidence of payments for the first and second quarters of 2023," Wamil said in response to questions from House prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan. "Second, based on its accomplishment report, it indicated that rewards had been paid, but the OVP did not submit any document evidencing the success of the information-gathering or surveillance activities resulting from the information provided by the informant, in violation of the joint circular," he added. article.title: Sara Duterte's impeachment trial, Week 5: Beyond the receipts
article.description: Five weeks into the trial, the proceedings have become about more than the fate of one elected official. They have evolved into an examination of how the Philippine government accounts for billions of pesos in confidential funds and whether the existing safeguards are sufficient to protect public money from misuse.

text.preview: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. Three days of testimony from Commission on Audit auditor Roderick Wamil, formerly assigned to the agency’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office, has shifted the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte from a largely political spectacle into a searching examination of confidential fund safeguards. In the process, the Senate impeachment court has exposed not only the strengths and weaknesses of the prosecution’s case but also the institutional gaps that have long surrounded the auditing of secret government expenditures. The proceedings from Days 11 to 13 demonstrate why impeachment trials should never be judged by dramatic courtroom exchanges alone. Beneath the debate over acknowledgment receipts, unusual names and missing documents lies a more consequential question: Has the prosecution shown that Duterte committed an impeachable offense, or has it primarily revealed deficiencies in the government’s auditing framework? Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro repeatedly says the prosecution’s case does not hinge on whether the names were aliases or genuine persons. “The important issue is accountability. Public officials entrusted with confidential funds must account for how public money was spent,” she said in an online press briefing on Thursday. Wamil’s testimony unquestionably advanced the prosecution’s case. Drawing from his audit of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, he detailed what COA considered repeated violations of Joint Circular No. 2015-01 — crafted in 2015 by COA, Department of Budget and Management, Department of the Interior and Local Government, the Government Commission for Government-Owned and Controlled Corporations, and the Department of National Defense — governing confidential and intelligence funds. article.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial, Week 8: Who knew where the confidential funds went?
article.description: Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent.

text.preview: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. The eighth week of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial ended with the Senate impeachment court focusing on a basic question: Who knew where the P500 million confidential funds went? Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent. Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio, the OVP assistant chief of staff, gave the most important testimony of the week. He told the court that Duterte knew about and authorized the activities involving confidential funds under her office. Asked by Presiding Officer Francis Escudero whether Duterte knew, supervised and authorized the entire process, from requesting the funds and withdrawing them to their release, spending, liquidation and responses to the Commission on Audit, Ortonio answered: “Yes, Your Honor.” His testimony followed two days of questioning of Gina Acosta, Duterte’s former special disbursing officer, now a staff officer VI at the OVP. A system of trust, or a break in accountability? Acosta said she released P125 million in cash to Lachica on Duterte’s instructions in December 2022. The money was the first tranche of the P500 million in OVP confidential funds now under scrutiny, disbursed from December 2022 to September 2023. But Acosta admitted that she did not personally know how Lachica spent the money. She said she relied on the documents he gave her when she prepared the liquidation reports. The prosecution has questioned whether this arrangement broke the chain of accountability for public funds. article.title: Who are the COA witnesses testifying on Sara Duterte confidential funds? | ABS-CBN News
article.description: On the sixth week of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the prosecution presented two witnesses from the Commission on Audit: Roderick Wamil

text.preview: State auditors Xylene Mae del Campo and Roderick Wamil. Maria Tan, ABS-CBN News MANILA — On the sixth week of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the prosecution presented two witnesses from the Commission on Audit: Roderick Wamil and Xylene Mae del Campo. Who is Roderick Wamil? Wamil, 34, currently serves as an audit team leader at COA-Pasay City. He has been with the commission for more than 11 years, having joined in 2014. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Accountancy from Central Luzon State University and his Juris Doctor degree from Arellano University. Before assuming his current post, Wamil served as a state auditor under the COA-Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO). WRAP: Tense exchanges as state auditor Wamil wraps up testimony His testimony focused on his experience auditing confidential fund disbursements, a key part of the prosecution's effort to establish alleged irregularities under Article I, which accuses Duterte of misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds. Wamil audited the Office of the Vice President's (OVP) liquidation of confidential funds for the fourth quarter of 2022 and the first, second, and third quarters of 2023. He also audited the Department of Education’s confidential funds during the first three quarters of 2023, when Duterte concurrently served as Education secretary. In February 2024, Wamil was reassigned to another office within the COA. Who is Xylene Mae del Campo? Following Wamil’s testimony, the prosecution presented its second COA witness, Xylene Mae del Campo. Del Campo, 36, is as a state auditor at the COA-ICFAO, succeeding Wamil in the position. She took over the audits of the OVP and DepEd confidential funds after Wamil’s transfer in February 2024. article.title: EXPLAINER: What is 'evidence of success' in the use of confidential funds?
article.description: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has entered its second month, with the Senate impeachment court now delving into the technical details surrounding the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Article I.

text.preview: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has entered its second month, with the Senate impeachment court now delving into the technical details surrounding the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Article I. One of the key terms that surfaced during the proceedings is "evidence of success." What does "evidence of success" mean? The term came up during the prosecution's questioning of state auditor Roderick Wamil, formerly of the Commission on Audit Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO), the office that audited confidential and intelligence funds lodged with various government offices, including the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) under Duterte. During direct examination, Wamil testified that the OVP reported spending P42 million in confidential funds for the provision of medical and food aid from February 6 to March 29, 2023, and another P40 million for the same purpose from April 25 to June 30, 2023, for a total of P82 million. "Our findings, or observations, were that the OVP did not submit documentary evidence of payments for the first and second quarters of 2023," Wamil said in response to questions from House prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan. "Second, based on its accomplishment report, it indicated that rewards had been paid, but the OVP did not submit any document evidencing the success of the information-gathering or surveillance activities resulting from the information provided by the informant, in violation of the joint circular," he added. text.preview: Lawyer Roderick Wamil, a former state auditor with the Commission on Audit’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO), returned to the witness stand on Tuesday to testify on the disbursement of more than P200 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) during Vice President Sara Duterte’s tenure as education secretary. Prosecution During the prosecution's presentation of evidence, Wamil testified that at least P129 million of the OVP's P250-million confidential fund allocation for the first and second quarters of 2023 lacked supporting documents proving that the disbursements were made for their intended purposes, in violation of Joint Circular No. 2015-01 governing the use of confidential and intelligence funds. According to Wamil, the unsupported disbursements included purchases of medicines and food assistance, as well as the payment of rewards and incentives for travel related to confidential operations, whose authenticity could not be verified due to the absence of the required documentation. article.title: Palace: Reinforce security ahead of BARMM election
article.description: The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday. Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos has directed concerned agencies to ensure a peaceful, orderly and credible conduct of the BARMM polls on Sept. 14. Castro clarified that the reported killings in BARMM since the start of the year were not related to the upcoming polls, and instead involved personal conflicts, citing information from the Commission on Elections. She said the Comelec, Philippine National Police (PNP) and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) are conducting focused law enforcement operations against private armed groups and other security threats in the region. Marcos earlier assured the Bangsamoro people that the first parliamentary election would push through as scheduled. Castro said 8,299 PNP personnel would be deployed in BARMM for election security. She added that the number may be augmented as the election approaches, depending on the PNP’s threat assessment and the Comelec requirements. “The PNP is working alongside the AFP and the Philippine Coast Guard to boost security, particularly in election areas of concern identified by the Comelec, to ensure the safe, peaceful and orderly conduct of the election,” Castro said. Meanwhile, 12 people have been arrested for violating the Comelec gun ban, as security operations intensify. PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez said the arrests came as police continue implementing security measures during the campaign period, noting that no violent election-related incident has been reported so far. “We have already laid out and are implementing our security operations,” Nartatez said. article.title: DOJ prosecutors seek raps vs Basilan mayor over 2025 poll attack
article.description: State prosecutors in the Bangsamoro region had recommended the filing of criminal cases against a mayor in Basilan and several others for their alleged involvement in a deadly election-related gun attack hours before the May 12, 2025 polling day.

text.preview: COTABATO CITY, Philippines — State prosecutors in the Bangsamoro region had recommended the filing of criminal cases against a mayor in Basilan and several others for their alleged involvement in a deadly election-related gun attack hours before the May 12, 2025 polling day. Radio reports on Friday, August 7, stated that the resolution of the Regional Prosecution Office 14 mentioned Arsina Kahing Nanoh, mayor of Hadji Muhtamad, her husband Nadz Nanoh, and relatives Walihiul Allama, Hadji Rahim Kahim, Lucman Kahim, Tudy Bayro, Sing Hassan and several others, tagged only as “john does,” as respondents to the three counts of murder, two counts of frustrated murder and attempted murder that prosecutors are to file in a court. The RPO 14 of the Department of Justice covers the five provinces in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Maguindanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, and the cities of Lamitan, Marawi and Cotabato, where the BARMM regional capitol is located. Copies of the RPO 14's resolution pertaining to its case buildup against Nano, one of the 11 municipal mayors in Basilan, and several others, were obtained on Wednesday by reporters from officials of the Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Camp SK Pendatun in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte and the military’s Western Mindanao Command based in Zamboanga City. The resolution, dated July 2, 2026, was signed by four officials of RPO 14. Regional police officials said the case that the BARMM regional prosecutors have recommended for filing in court against the respondents is related to the offshore attack before dawn on May 12 last year in the sea close to the beachfront Barangay Sangbay Big in Hadji Muhtamad by gunmen riding speedboats, allegedly owned by the mayor, of supporters and poll watchers of then mayoral candidate Hadji Jamar Abdullah Mansul. articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial, Week 8: Who knew where the confidential funds went?
articles.description: Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent.

text.preview: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. The eighth week of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial ended with the Senate impeachment court focusing on a basic question: Who knew where the P500 million confidential funds went? Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent. Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio, the OVP assistant chief of staff, gave the most important testimony of the week. He told the court that Duterte knew about and authorized the activities involving confidential funds under her office. Asked by Presiding Officer Francis Escudero whether Duterte knew, supervised and authorized the entire process, from requesting the funds and withdrawing them to their release, spending, liquidation and responses to the Commission on Audit, Ortonio answered: “Yes, Your Honor.” His testimony followed two days of questioning of Gina Acosta, Duterte’s former special disbursing officer, now a staff officer VI at the OVP. A system of trust, or a break in accountability? Acosta said she released P125 million in cash to Lachica on Duterte’s instructions in December 2022. The money was the first tranche of the P500 million in OVP confidential funds now under scrutiny, disbursed from December 2022 to September 2023. But Acosta admitted that she did not personally know how Lachica spent the money. She said she relied on the documents he gave her when she prepared the liquidation reports. The prosecution has questioned whether this arrangement broke the chain of accountability for public funds. Senator-judge Robinhood Padilla asked former state auditor Roderick Wamil if he had ever visited the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and whether he was aware of the country's ongoing terrorism threats.
During his interjection, Padilla raised preliminary questions about the Audit Observation Memorandum, trying to establish ties to the confidential funds used by Vice President Sara Duterte for surveillance on potential New People's Army (NPA) recruitment.
"But you are the one handling the investigation regarding the confidential funds, is that correct?" Padilla asked Wamil.

"Do you believe that confidential agents should identify themselves? State their real names," the senator furthered.
"There are no provisions regarding that in the joint circular," Wamil said.
Padilla then asked Wamil to define "confidential," to which the auditor replied, "classified."

output.title: Who are the COA witnesses testifying on Sara Duterte confidential funds? | ABS-CBN News
output.description: On the sixth week of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the prosecution presented two witnesses from the Commission on Audit: Roderick Wamil
output.text: State auditors Xylene Mae del Campo and Roderick Wamil. Maria Tan, ABS-CBN News MANILA — On the sixth week of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the prosecution presented two witnesses from the Commission on Audit: Roderick Wamil and Xylene Mae del Campo. Who is Roderick Wamil? Wamil, 34, currently serves as an audit team leader at COA-Pasay City. He has been with the commission for more than 11 years, having joined in 2014. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Accountancy from Central Luzon State University and his Juris Doctor degree from Arellano University. Before assuming his current post, Wamil served as a state auditor under the COA-Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO). WRAP: Tense exchanges as state auditor Wamil wraps up testimony His testimony focused on his experience auditing confidential fund disbursements, a key part of the prosecution's effort to establish alleged irregularities under Article I, which accuses Duterte of misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds. Wamil audited the Office of the Vice President's (OVP) liquidation of confidential funds for the fourth quarter of 2022 and the first, second, and third quarters of 2023. He also audited the Department of Education’s confidential funds during the first three quarters of 2023, when Duterte concurrently served as Education secretary. In February 2024, Wamil was reassigned to another office within the COA. Who is Xylene Mae del Campo? Following Wamil’s testimony, the prosecution presented its second COA witness, Xylene Mae del Campo. Del Campo, 36, is as a state auditor at the COA-ICFAO, succeeding Wamil in the position. She took over the audits of the OVP and DepEd confidential funds after Wamil’s transfer in February 2024. "Siya po ang nagtuloy ng inumpisahan ni Mr. Wamil na evaluation ng confidential funds," prosecution private counsel Lorna Kapunan said on Wednesday, August 6. (She continued Wamil's evaluation of confidential funds.) Suspension notice presumes confidential funds used for personal benefit: COA auditor Del Campo earned her Bachelor of Science in Accountancy from Saint Louis University. She has been with the COA for 12 years, having started as a state auditor in August 2014. She was the state auditor who evaluated the response of the OVP to the first COA notice of suspension in December 2023 in relation to its confidential funds for December 2022. She is scheduled to again take the witness stand next week, on Monday, August 10. COA: Use of aliases in confidential fund receipts 'neither allowed nor prohibited' RELATED VIDEOS:

output.title: Padilla tests auditor on knowledge of terrorism, security threats | ABS-CBN News
output.description: Senator Robin Padilla on Wednesday questioned former Commission on Audit (COA) state auditor Roderick Wamil about his familiarity with terrorism and security th
output.text: MANILA — Sen. Robin Padilla on Wednesday questioned state auditor Roderick Wamil on his familiarity with terrorism and with security threats as he stressed the importance of confidential funds to address these issues. Wamil, previously assigned to the Commission on Audit-Internal Control and Fraud Audit Office, was testifying at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on audit findings on her offices' use of confidential funds. Padilla asked Wamil if he had been to parts of the country like the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, the Bicol region, and to Mindanao. Padilla also asked Wamil if he had visited remote communities and seen the challenges faced by residents there, including access to food and medicine. Wamil said he had been to mountainous areas but did not witness the conditions described by the senator. “Ayun, hindi kayo exposed," Padilla said. (Oh there, you are not exposed to that.) Auditor: Medicines ‘not normal’ reward for information in confidential operations ARMED GROUPS Padilla then shifted his questions to national security as he asked if Wamil was familiar with armed groups ISIS, Abu Sayyaf and the New People's Army. "Sa news po, nababalitaan ko," the auditor said. (I heard about them in the news.) “Alam niyo po ba kung gaano na kagrabe ang terrorism sa bansa?” Padilla asked. (Do you know how severe terrorism is in the country?) Wamil, an accountant and lawyer, responded he has "no threshold" to determine that Padilla said he asked because he heard that Wamil is in charge of investigating the use of confidential funds. Auditor says 'first time' to encounter confidential expenses backed only by acknowledgement receipts Wamil clarified that COA's role is to see if government agencies complied with rules on accounting for confidential fund expenditures.. "Hindi po siya investigation, evaluation siya," Wamil said. (It is not an investigation but an evaluation.) Padilla also pressed Wamil on the audit observations that he had raised. "Konklusyon po ba yun (Is that a conclusion)? Final? Final?" Padilla said as Wamil explained that the Audit Observation Memorandum he wrote on OVP spending was part of a preliminary stage of a COA audit. PADILLA LINKS CHECKS TO 'RED' ANNIVERSARIES In later questions, Padilla said that the dates of some confidential expenses that COA had flagged were close to the founding anniversaries of the Communist Party of the Philippines, the New People's Army and the National Democratic Front. He also said that "for the first time", there were no NPA attacks on those dates. Wamil said he has no personal knowledge on the supposed significance of the dates. "Ang tanong ko po, naniniwala po ba kayo na malaki ang papel ng confidential fund at confidential agent?" Padilla asked. (My question is, do you believe that confidential funds and confidential agents have an important role?) "Depende po 'yan sa ano po talaga 'yung mandate ng agency," Wamil replied. (That depends on the what the mandate of the agency is.)

output.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 12: Ex-auditor says P200M confidential funds lacked documents
output.description: Lawyer Roderick Wamil, a former state auditor with the Commission on Audit’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO), returned to the witness stand on Tuesday to testify on the disbursement of more than P200 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) during Vice President Sara Duterte’s tenure as education secretary.
output.text: Lawyer Roderick Wamil, a former state auditor with the Commission on Audit’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO), returned to the witness stand on Tuesday to testify on the disbursement of more than P200 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) during Vice President Sara Duterte’s tenure as education secretary. Prosecution During the prosecution's presentation of evidence, Wamil testified that at least P129 million of the OVP's P250-million confidential fund allocation for the first and second quarters of 2023 lacked supporting documents proving that the disbursements were made for their intended purposes, in violation of Joint Circular No. 2015-01 governing the use of confidential and intelligence funds. According to Wamil, the unsupported disbursements included purchases of medicines and food assistance, as well as the payment of rewards and incentives for travel related to confidential operations, whose authenticity could not be verified due to the absence of the required documentation. Wamil also testified that the Department of Education failed to submit supporting documents for the disbursement of P112.5 million in confidential funds in 2023, which were reportedly used for the following: Counter-insurgency programs (P9.375 million in Q1; P9.3 million in Q2; P9.2 million in Q3) Abuse prevention and control within schools (P10 million in Q1; P10.075 million in Q2; P10.125 million in Q3) Anti-illegal activities operations (P9 million in Q1; P9.1 million in Q2; P9.14 million in Q3) Anti-extremism/terrorism programs (P9.125 million in Q1; P9.025 million in Q2; P9.035 million in Q3) Further, Wamil said that the camp of Vice President Sara Duterte sought an exemption from a 2015 COA joint circular that sets the guidelines for auditing confidential funds by requesting that the commission issue an "audit query" instead of an Audit Observation Memorandum (AOM) for the agencies' disbursement of confidential funds. These accounts by Wamil prompted private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan to say that such confidential fund disbursement by the Vice President’s office and the DepEd under her leadership was a scam. The prosecution panel later said that Wamil’s testimony remains undisputed even amid cross-examination by the defense team. Defense In response, Poa presented a letter showing that Vice President Sara Duterte was not the only vice president to receive confidential funds, noting that then Vice President Jejomar Binay's office was also granted a confidential fund allocation in 2014. Poa argued that this contradicted Wamil's testimony that only Duterte had been given confidential funds as vice president. However, Binay's 2014 confidential fund allocation predated Joint Circular No. 2015-01, which was issued in 2015 and established the guidelines governing the use, liquidation, and audit of confidential and intelligence funds. Also on Tuesday, Poa asked the Senate impeachment court to strike Kapunan's scam comments off the record for being "out of line." His objection was sustained by Senate impeachment court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero. Poa argued that Wamil's findings that the disbursements failed to comply with the guidelines under Joint Circular No. 2015-01 were merely preliminary, as they were contained in an Audit Observation Memorandum (AOM). He stressed that the observations in an AOM do not, by themselves, establish that confidential funds were misused. Impeachment court Meanwhile, Escudero ordered the issuance of a new subpoena for COA-ICFAO official Xylene Del Campo, valid from August 5 to 11, 2026. She will be the next witness to be presented by the House prosecution panel to testify on Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds. Escudero likewise confirmed the receipt of the House prosecution panel’s motion for judicial notice, and ordered the Defense to either deliver an oral opposition or comment on the matter, or submit a written response by Wednesday. He also granted the request of the prosecution for a conference before the Clerk of Court for the rescheduling of the marking of evidence on Wednesday, August 5, at 4 pm. — With reports from Giselle Ombay and Sundy Locus/LDF GMA News

output.title: EXPLAINER: What is 'evidence of success' in the use of confidential funds?
output.description: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has entered its second month, with the Senate impeachment court now delving into the technical details surrounding the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Article I.
output.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has entered its second month, with the Senate impeachment court now delving into the technical details surrounding the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Article I. One of the key terms that surfaced during the proceedings is "evidence of success." What does "evidence of success" mean? The term came up during the prosecution's questioning of state auditor Roderick Wamil, formerly of the Commission on Audit Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (COA-ICFAO), the office that audited confidential and intelligence funds lodged with various government offices, including the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) under Duterte. During direct examination, Wamil testified that the OVP reported spending P42 million in confidential funds for the provision of medical and food aid from February 6 to March 29, 2023, and another P40 million for the same purpose from April 25 to June 30, 2023, for a total of P82 million. "Our findings, or observations, were that the OVP did not submit documentary evidence of payments for the first and second quarters of 2023," Wamil said in response to questions from House prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan. "Second, based on its accomplishment report, it indicated that rewards had been paid, but the OVP did not submit any document evidencing the success of the information-gathering or surveillance activities resulting from the information provided by the informant, in violation of the joint circular," he added. Under COA Joint Circular No. 2015-01, which sets the guidelines on the use of confidential and intelligence funds, CF is allocated to agencies for Confidential Expenses, or expenses for “surveillance activities in civilian government agencies that are intended to support the mandate or operations of the agency.” While spending from these funds is exempt from certain budgeting and auditing rules because of their sensitive nature, agencies are still required to comply with specific Commission on Audit (COA) guidelines to ensure the funds are properly used. READ: EXPLAINER: Understanding confidential funds and intelligence funds Wamil testified that the OVP failed to comply with all documentary requirements for the first and second quarters of 2023. As a result, COA issued the office an Audit Observation Memorandum (AOM). According to the AOM, the OVP paid P15 million in rewards to informants from February 6 to March 29, 2023, and another P12 million from April 25 to June 30, 2023. What does the COA require? Under COA Joint Circular No. 2015-01, which sets the guidelines on the use of confidential and intelligence funds, payments of rewards to informants must be: "supported with documents evidencing the success of the information gathering and/or surveillance activities on account of the information given by the informer." In other words, an agency that uses confidential funds to pay rewards to informants must be able to demonstrate that the information provided led to a successful surveillance or information-gathering activity. However, the joint circular does not prescribe a specific document that qualifies as evidence of success, according to Wamil. "No specific document is mentioned. What we look for is a causal link between the successful surveillance or information-gathering activity and the information provided by the informer," he said. Wamil explained that COA requires such evidence to verify that the rewards paid to informants are justified and that public funds were used for their intended purpose. — MCG GMA News

output.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial, Week 8: Who knew where the confidential funds went?
output.description: Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent.
output.text: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. The eighth week of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial ended with the Senate impeachment court focusing on a basic question: Who knew where the P500 million confidential funds went? Over three days —the 17th, 18th and 19th days of the trial — the testimony from two ranking officials of the Office of the Vice President pointed to Duterte and her former security chief, Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, as the two people with the clearest knowledge of how the funds were handled and spent. Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio, the OVP assistant chief of staff, gave the most important testimony of the week. He told the court that Duterte knew about and authorized the activities involving confidential funds under her office. Asked by Presiding Officer Francis Escudero whether Duterte knew, supervised and authorized the entire process, from requesting the funds and withdrawing them to their release, spending, liquidation and responses to the Commission on Audit, Ortonio answered: “Yes, Your Honor.” His testimony followed two days of questioning of Gina Acosta, Duterte’s former special disbursing officer, now a staff officer VI at the OVP. A system of trust, or a break in accountability? Acosta said she released P125 million in cash to Lachica on Duterte’s instructions in December 2022. The money was the first tranche of the P500 million in OVP confidential funds now under scrutiny, disbursed from December 2022 to September 2023. But Acosta admitted that she did not personally know how Lachica spent the money. She said she relied on the documents he gave her when she prepared the liquidation reports. The prosecution has questioned whether this arrangement broke the chain of accountability for public funds. Acosta acknowledged that Lachica was not a bonded OVP disbursing officer when she turned over the money to him. The prosecution tried to show that the same system may have existed when Duterte was still mayor of Davao City. Acosta testified that confidential funds there were also turned over to a security officer for implementation. The suggestion is that the practice may have followed Duterte from Davao City to the OVP. The impeachment court, however, has yet to rule that these practices amounted to misuse of public funds or violated government rules. The knowledge gap at the top By Day 19, the questioning became more direct. Ortonio said he had no personal knowledge of how the confidential funds were spent, where the money went or which OVP programs received it. He said he had no role in preparing liquidation reports, disbursing the money or recording the expenses. Escudero then pointed out an apparent gap in the OVP’s chain of knowledge. Ortonio confirmed that Duterte, chief of staff Zuleika Lopez and himself were the OVP’s three highest-ranking officials. Yet he agreed that he did not know how the confidential funds were actually used. “Col. Lachica,” Ortonio said, knew the implementation as the security officer. This meant that, based on the testimony, Duterte knew and authorized the activities as head of the agency, while Lachica knew how the operations were implemented on the ground. On questioning by Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros, Ortonio said that Duterte was given copies and information related to the confidential funds and that documents sent to COA carried her final approval. Asked whether Duterte was therefore the person most responsible, Ortonio said that, as head of the agency, he would say so. The defense repeatedly objected to questions it considered misleading, vague or speculative. But Ortonio’s testimony, much of it elicited by Escudero and other senator-judges, pushed Duterte’s role to the center of the trial. That also made Lachica’s absence from the witness stand even more noticeable. Acosta repeatedly identified him as the person who received the cash and implemented the confidential activities. Yet neither she nor Ortonio could directly explain to the court how the money was actually spent. Acosta said she did not personally see Lachica give money to the supposed recipients listed in acknowledgment receipts. Ortonio said he had no personal knowledge of where the funds went. On Tuesday, Lachica issued a brief statement through the OVP, saying he is ready to “tell the truth” if lawfully called to testify, subject to security restrictions. But the prosecution has not yet decided whether to call him as a hostile witness. That leaves a major question hanging over the case: If Lachica was the person who implemented the activities, will the court hear directly from him about where the money went? The prosecution has placed him at the center of the money trail without yet putting him on the witness stand. Court draws a line on sub judice Day 19 also brought an important ruling on public comments about the trial. Escudero laid down clearer rules on sub judice, prohibiting senator-judges and lawyers from both sides from making public statements about the substance or merits of the case. The ruling came after complaints over public and social media comments by lawyers involved in the proceedings. Escudero said earlier violations would not be punished, but warned that the rules would be enforced from now on. Lawyers who violate the rule face a two-strike system. The first offense brings a public reprimand and stern warning. A second offense may result in a P30,000 fine and possible restrictions on speaking, objecting or examining witnesses during the trial. Senator-judges may continue asking questions, but Escudero said they must do so with “cold neutrality.” The senator-judges have become increasingly active in questioning witnesses, often probing issues that neither side has fully explored. Padilla’s alias argument, and Bam’s quick rebuttal Another major issue was the use of aliases in documents covering confidential fund transactions. Sen. Robinhood Padilla argued that using an alias was not unusual, pointing to national heroes and political figures who used pseudonyms. He mentioned Andres Bonifacio, Jose Rizal and former Sen. Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr., who used the alias “Marcial Bonifacio.” But Sen. Bam Aquino quickly pointed out the difference. Yes, Ninoy used an alias, he said. But he did not receive confidential funds. That exchange captured the real issue before the impeachment court. The question is not simply whether aliases can be used in confidential operations. The bigger question is whether the names on the acknowledgment receipts belonged to real people, whether those people actually received the money, and whether the payments were for legitimate confidential activities. Senator-judge Panfilo Lacson suggested that the court may eventually subpoena documents to settle the issue. Escudero said the impeachment court had the power to do so at the appropriate time. The trail now leads to two people Ortonio’s testimony made the lines of responsibility clearer. Acosta placed Lachica at the center of the actual implementation and spending. Ortonio placed Duterte at the top of the chain of knowledge, authorization and approval. The prosecution must still prove what actually happened to the money and whether any laws or rules were violated. But after three days of testimony, the case appears to have narrowed to a crucial gap in the evidence. The person who authorized the activities was the vice president. The person who implemented them was her security chief. The next question for the impeachment court is whether it will get a complete answer from either, or both, about exactly where the money went. output.title: Sara Duterte's impeachment trial, Week 5: Beyond the receipts
output.description: Five weeks into the trial, the proceedings have become about more than the fate of one elected official. They have evolved into an examination of how the Philippine government accounts for billions of pesos in confidential funds and whether the existing safeguards are sufficient to protect public money from misuse.
output.text: Tita C. Valderama is an editor and trustee of VERA Files. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years. Three days of testimony from Commission on Audit auditor Roderick Wamil, formerly assigned to the agency’s Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office, has shifted the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte from a largely political spectacle into a searching examination of confidential fund safeguards. In the process, the Senate impeachment court has exposed not only the strengths and weaknesses of the prosecution’s case but also the institutional gaps that have long surrounded the auditing of secret government expenditures. The proceedings from Days 11 to 13 demonstrate why impeachment trials should never be judged by dramatic courtroom exchanges alone. Beneath the debate over acknowledgment receipts, unusual names and missing documents lies a more consequential question: Has the prosecution shown that Duterte committed an impeachable offense, or has it primarily revealed deficiencies in the government’s auditing framework? Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro repeatedly says the prosecution’s case does not hinge on whether the names were aliases or genuine persons. “The important issue is accountability. Public officials entrusted with confidential funds must account for how public money was spent,” she said in an online press briefing on Thursday. Wamil’s testimony unquestionably advanced the prosecution’s case. Drawing from his audit of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, he detailed what COA considered repeated violations of Joint Circular No. 2015-01 — crafted in 2015 by COA, Department of Budget and Management, Department of the Interior and Local Government, the Government Commission for Government-Owned and Controlled Corporations, and the Department of National Defense — governing confidential and intelligence funds. These included expenditures unsupported by official receipts, purchases allegedly outside the list of authorized confidential expenses, the absence of documents proving successful intelligence operations before rewards were paid, and liquidation reports that failed to specify the confidential activities for which the funds were supposedly spent. Most significant was his testimony that Duterte, as head of both the OVP and DepEd at one point, was the accountable officer for the confidential funds released to the two offices in 2022 and 2023. Wamil explained that under the joint circular, failure to properly liquidate confidential funds creates a prima facie presumption that the accountable officer used the money for personal benefit. That statement became one of the prosecution’s strongest legal anchors. Impeachment under Article XI of the Constitution is ultimately about public accountability, not merely accounting procedures. The House prosecutors are trying to convince the senator-judges that the alleged deficiencies in the liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds constitute a betrayal of public trust. Yet the defense’s cross-examination also illustrated why audit findings cannot automatically translate into constitutional liability. Defense counsel Michael Poa managed to elicit from Wamil that nothing in Joint Circular No. 2015-01 prohibits an agency from spending an entire quarterly confidential fund allocation within 11 days. Wamil also admitted that COA itself did not characterize the rapid disbursement of the funds as an audit violation, noting that the timing merely appeared as a factual observation in the Audit Observation Memorandum. Those admissions are significant because much of the public narrative since 2024 has focused on how quickly the OVP spent P125 million in confidential funds. The prosecution has been trying to prove that the expenditures violated auditing rules or that the liquidation documents failed to demonstrate legitimate confidential operations, as shown by questionable receipts such as rental for safehouses at P2 million a day and P70,000 worth of medicines as reward for Mary Grace Piattos in exchange for intelligence information. Apart from the issue of accountability, the prosecution also focused on authenticity. The proceedings took a more intriguing turn when senator-judges examined the acknowledgment receipts bearing unusual names such as Mary Grace Piattos, Mico Harina, Andy Lim and Alejandro Pikit. While the defense has yet to clearly state whether the names appearing in the liquidation documents were aliases or real individuals, the prosecutors have long been referring to these as fictitious. “These can be aliases, but these are really fictitious names,” quipped prosecution counsel Kapunan. “Senators will be surprised when their names are also there.” She said there were even “fruit salad” names, such as Mango and Keso. During the House investigations in 2024, subpoenaed documents from COA showed 405 alleged aliases were used in liquidating the OVPs confidential funds and 677 in the Department of Education’s confidential funds. Eleven of these names surfaced during Tuesday’s trial, including Piattos, Harina, Lim, Pikit, Nova Santos, Patty Ting, and Feonna Biong. However, Wamil admitted that the audit was entirely document-based and that verifying whether the names on the acknowledgement receipts to liquidate confidential funds were aliases or real persons “was not part of the audit.” Asked repeatedly by senator-judges whether COA had verified that the names belonged to actual persons, Wamil replied that auditors did not undertake such verification because Joint Circular No. 2015-01 is silent on the use of aliases or code names. Their audit was confined to determining compliance with documentary requirements, not establishing the true identities of the individuals listed in the acknowledgment receipts. For the defense, Wamil’s testimony undercuts any claim that COA itself determined the names were fictitious. Wamil never testified that the recipients did not exist; he simply acknowledged that auditors did not investigate that issue. For the prosecution, however, the testimony exposes a far more troubling institutional problem. If auditors are neither authorized nor required to verify whether listed recipients actually exist, then the government’s oversight of confidential funds depends largely on documentary compliance. Such a framework may satisfy procedural requirements while leaving ample room for abuse. It is therefore unsurprising that several senator-judges shifted their focus from Duterte’s conduct to the limitations of the auditing system itself. Senator-judge Panfilo Lacson questioned why COA remains confined to what he described as “paper audits,” suggesting auditors should be granted authority and security clearances to examine classified operational records. Senator-judge Bam Aquino asked whether the rules should expressly address the use of aliases, while Senator-judge Juan Miguel Zubiri emphasized that confidential funds remain public funds and should not be insulated from meaningful scrutiny simply because they finance confidential operations. Those exchanges may prove to be one of the trial’s most enduring contributions. Whatever verdict the Senate eventually reaches, the proceedings have exposed weaknesses in Joint Circular No. 2015-01 that Congress and COA can no longer afford to ignore. The defense, meanwhile, appears to be pursuing a strategy that places equal emphasis on procedure and substance. Its refusal to stipulate to the authenticity of more than 4,000 acknowledgment receipts is more than a procedural maneuver. By requiring the prosecution to authenticate each document, the defense seeks to ensure that every piece of documentary evidence satisfies the rules before it is considered by the impeachment court. The defense has maintained that it is not claiming the receipts are fabricated; rather, it argues that the sheer volume of loose documents prevents it from conceding their authenticity without careful examination. The strategy could substantially prolong the trial, way beyond the allotted 92 days for the presentation of evidence: 62 days for the prosecution and 30 days for the defense. Every contested acknowledgment receipt will require proper authentication, consuming valuable hearing time and compelling prosecutors to build the evidentiary chain document by document. While this may test the patience of both the senator-judges and the public, it also underscores a fundamental principle of due process: no party should be required to admit the authenticity of documents it has not fully examined. The Senate impeachment court’s decision to allow the defense additional time to review the documents suggests an appreciation of that balance between efficiency and fairness. Next week, attention would turn to supervising COA auditor Xylene del Campo, whose testimony is expected to continue the prosecution’s effort to establish the integrity—or lack thereof—of the liquidation process. Her appearance may prove pivotal. If she is able to reinforce Wamil’s findings with additional documentary evidence, the prosecution could strengthen its argument that the questioned transactions reflected more than procedural lapses. If not, the defense may succeed in portraying the case as one built largely on audit deficiencies rather than proof of impeachable misconduct. The coming hearings will therefore determine whether the prosecution can bridge the gap between administrative findings and constitutional accountability. Five weeks into the trial, the proceedings have become about more than the fate of one elected official. They have evolved into an examination of how the Philippine government accounts for billions of pesos in confidential funds and whether the existing safeguards are sufficient to protect public money from misuse. That may prove to be the trial’s most significant legacy. Whatever verdict the Senate impeachment court ultimately renders, the proceedings have already demonstrated that accountability cannot rest solely on paperwork, nor can secrecy excuse weak oversight. Public officials entrusted with confidential funds deserve rules that are both workable and rigorous, while taxpayers deserve assurance that confidentiality does not become a shield against accountability. The impeachment court’s task is to determine whether Sara Duterte should be held constitutionally liable. The broader challenge belongs to Congress and the Commission on Audit: to ensure that, after this impeachment trial ends, the country’s system for auditing confidential funds is no longer judged merely by the receipts, but by its ability to inspire public confidence Receive fresh perspectives and explainers in your inbox every Tuesday and Friday.

output.title: Palace: Reinforce security ahead of BARMM election
output.description: The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday.
output.text: MANILA, Philippines — The government is set to reinforce security in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao as the first-ever BARMM parliamentary election approaches, Malacañang said yesterday. Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos has directed concerned agencies to ensure a peaceful, orderly and credible conduct of the BARMM polls on Sept. 14. Castro clarified that the reported killings in BARMM since the start of the year were not related to the upcoming polls, and instead involved personal conflicts, citing information from the Commission on Elections. She said the Comelec, Philippine National Police (PNP) and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) are conducting focused law enforcement operations against private armed groups and other security threats in the region. Marcos earlier assured the Bangsamoro people that the first parliamentary election would push through as scheduled. Castro said 8,299 PNP personnel would be deployed in BARMM for election security. She added that the number may be augmented as the election approaches, depending on the PNP’s threat assessment and the Comelec requirements. “The PNP is working alongside the AFP and the Philippine Coast Guard to boost security, particularly in election areas of concern identified by the Comelec, to ensure the safe, peaceful and orderly conduct of the election,” Castro said. Meanwhile, 12 people have been arrested for violating the Comelec gun ban, as security operations intensify. PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez said the arrests came as police continue implementing security measures during the campaign period, noting that no violent election-related incident has been reported so far. “We have already laid out and are implementing our security operations,” Nartatez said. output.title: DOJ prosecutors seek raps vs Basilan mayor over 2025 poll attack
output.description: State prosecutors in the Bangsamoro region had recommended the filing of criminal cases against a mayor in Basilan and several others for their alleged involvement in a deadly election-related gun attack hours before the May 12, 2025 polling day.
output.text: COTABATO CITY, Philippines — State prosecutors in the Bangsamoro region had recommended the filing of criminal cases against a mayor in Basilan and several others for their alleged involvement in a deadly election-related gun attack hours before the May 12, 2025 polling day. Radio reports on Friday, August 7, stated that the resolution of the Regional Prosecution Office 14 mentioned Arsina Kahing Nanoh, mayor of Hadji Muhtamad, her husband Nadz Nanoh, and relatives Walihiul Allama, Hadji Rahim Kahim, Lucman Kahim, Tudy Bayro, Sing Hassan and several others, tagged only as “john does,” as respondents to the three counts of murder, two counts of frustrated murder and attempted murder that prosecutors are to file in a court. The RPO 14 of the Department of Justice covers the five provinces in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Maguindanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, and the cities of Lamitan, Marawi and Cotabato, where the BARMM regional capitol is located. Copies of the RPO 14's resolution pertaining to its case buildup against Nano, one of the 11 municipal mayors in Basilan, and several others, were obtained on Wednesday by reporters from officials of the Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Camp SK Pendatun in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte and the military’s Western Mindanao Command based in Zamboanga City. The resolution, dated July 2, 2026, was signed by four officials of RPO 14. Regional police officials said the case that the BARMM regional prosecutors have recommended for filing in court against the respondents is related to the offshore attack before dawn on May 12 last year in the sea close to the beachfront Barangay Sangbay Big in Hadji Muhtamad by gunmen riding speedboats, allegedly owned by the mayor, of supporters and poll watchers of then mayoral candidate Hadji Jamar Abdullah Mansul. The attack left three passengers of the pumpboat, Ben Bakil, Murasidol Abdurahman and Samir Jamiri Allil dead and two others, Habir Alih and Saldi Alih, wounded. Mansul was defeated by Nanoh in the 2025 mayoral race in Hadji Muhtamad. Regional Prosecutors had stated that while Nanoh, then seeking reelection, was not at the scene, it is assumed that she was part of the conspiracy to harm the victims owing to his alleged ownership of the speedboats used in the atrocity and her close relationship with its alleged perpetrators. Reporters in BARMM provinces and cities tried, but failed to reach the mayor for comment. Philstar.com is one of the most vibrant, opinionated, discerning communities of readers on cyberspace.
